section_1.title: The Hook: Geometry vs. Topology
section_1.content: Define topology as 'rubber-sheet geometry.' Explain that unlike standard geometry (which cares about distances and angles), topology ignores stretching and bending, focusing only on properties that remain invariant under continuous deformation.
section_1.example: Visualize a coffee mug and a donut made of play-dough. Show an animation where the mug is smoothly molded into the shape of a donut without tearing or gluing.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Concept: Homeomorphism
section_2.content: Introduce the concept of 'Homeomorphism.' Two objects are topologically equivalent if one can be transformed into the other via a continuous deformation (bijective mapping). Crucially, we cannot tear, cut, or glue the shape.
section_2.example: Display an animation of a square being stretched into a circle. Because we can map every point on the square to the circle without cutting, they are homeomorphic.

section_3.title: The Key Invariant: Genus (The 'Hole' Count)
section_3.content: Explain that the number of holes is a fundamental topological invariant. This integer is called the 'genus.' Objects with different numbers of holes are topologically distinct.
section_3.example: Compare a soccer ball (Genus 0, no holes), a donut (Genus 1, one hole), and a pair of glasses (Genus 2, two holes/loops). Explain why a soccer ball can never be turned into a donut without puncturing it.

section_4.title: The Famous Application: The Euler Characteristic
section_4.content: Briefly introduce the formula V - E + F = 2 (Vertices - Edges + Faces). Explain how this formula stays constant for any convex polyhedron regardless of its specific shape, proving it is a topological property.
section_4.example: Show a cube and a tetrahedron. Count their vertices, edges, and faces to demonstrate that they both result in 2, illustrating that they share the same underlying 'topological DNA'.

section_5.title: Real-World Conclusion: Why Topology Matters
section_5.content: Summarize how topology is used in modern science, from DNA supercoiling in biology to networking and data analysis. Final thought: Topology allows us to categorize complex shapes by their simplest, most persistent traits.
section_5.example: Mention how a biologist identifies 'knots' in DNA strands, or how a roboticist plans a path for a robot arm by mapping the 'topological space' of its joints.

        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]

        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)

                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
